US-119-HR6380.title: Chiricahua National Park Act
US-119-HR6380.summary:
Chiricahua National Park Act

This bill redesignates the Chiricahua National Monument in Arizona as the Chiricahua National Park.

The bill directs the National Park Service (NPS) to (1) ensure the protection of traditional cultural and religious sites in the park, and (2) provide access to those sites by members of Indian tribes for traditional cultural and customary uses.

Upon the request of an Indian tribe, the NPS may temporarily close to general public use one or more specific areas of the park to protect traditional cultural and customary uses in the area by members of the tribe. The closure must be limited to the smallest practicable area for the minimum period necessary for the traditional cultural and religious activities.

US-119-HR10680.description: To direct the Secretary of Health and Human Services to establish a grant program to facilitate food access in community health centers, and for other purposes.
US-119-HR10680.aiSummary: The bill would direct the Health and Human Services Secretary to set up a grant program to help community health centers improve food access. It would let partnerships between a community health center and a nonprofit food group apply for grants for things like a food space, a food vehicle, or related costs. Each grant could be up to $500,000, and the department would have to share reports on the program’s results and effect on patients.

US-119-HR9394.title: Civil Preparedness for Agroterrorism Exercise Act of 2026
US-119-HR9394.summary:
Civil Preparedness for Agroterrorism Exercise Act of 2026

This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within four years after the bill’s enactment, to conduct an exercise to enhance collective domestic prevention, response, and recovery regarding acts of agroterrorism (i.e., terrorism targeting or threatening agriculture and food systems of vital importance to national security, public health, or safety). The scenario in the exercise must involve agroterrorists transporting and deploying in the United States a biological agent (e.g., microorganism or infectious substance) capable of harming critical agriculture and food operations and must address how relevant public and private entities can coordinate to develop preparedness and mitigate widespread disruption.

Within 180 days after completion of the exercise, DHS must submit to Congress an after-action report including the findings of the exercise, plans for incorporating lessons learned into future operations, and recommended legislative actions.

US-119-HR10163.title: American Quantum Competitiveness Act
US-119-HR10163.summary:
American Quantum Competitiveness Act

This bill requires the Department of Commerce to advise the President on, and support U.S. commercial leadership related to, quantum technology and related supply chains. (Quantum technology uses the law of quantum physics for advanced information processing.)

Specifically, Commerce must serve as principal advisor to the President on (1) commercial manufacturing, deployment, and scaling of quantum technology; (2) the supply of critical components of quantum technology; and (3) the establishment, maintenance, and resiliency of a trusted quantum supply chain. (A trusted quantum supply chain involves the sourcing of critical components from the United States or a trusted supplier that is domiciled, headquartered, and organized in the United States or a foreign country that meets specified criteria.)

In advising the President on the quantum supply chain, Commerce must
• use existing authorities or programs to promote a trusted supply chain;
• identify and address barriers to investment in a trusted supply chain; and
• establish a mechanism for identifying critical components, assessing their availability, and mitigating risks related to acquiring them from China, Iran, North Korea, or Russia.

Commerce must also support U.S. commercial leadership in quantum technology and critical components, including by promoting private investment in commercial quantum efforts.

Commerce must periodically publish reports that include a comprehensive strategy for advancing a trusted quantum supply chain and U.S. commercial leadership in quantum technology and critical components.

Introduced in House

US-119-HR10020.description: To amend title XVIII of the Social Security Act to establish a Medicare home care benefit, and for other purposes.
US-119-HR10020.aiSummary: The bill would add a Medicare home care benefit for people on Medicare who need help with daily tasks at home. It would cover up to 20 hours a week of help like bathing, dressing, meal prep, medicine reminders, and light housework tied to health and safety. The bill would also raise Part B premiums to cover the new benefit and would apply to services furnished on or after the first day of the first plan year beginning more than 2 years after enactment.

US-119-HR9790.description: To expand access to methadone through alternative care models using pharmacies.
US-119-HR9790.aiSummary: The bill would let certain qualified doctors and other prescribers write methadone for opioid use disorder so it can be filled at a pharmacy. It would use electronic prescriptions, require informed consent, and allow telemedicine for some treatment, while still keeping other care through opioid treatment programs. States could ask the Attorney General to stop this registration in that state, and pharmacies would not need a separate registration to dispense the medicine. The changes would take effect 180 days after enactment.

US-119-S222.title: Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act of 2025
US-119-S222.summary:
Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act of 2025

This act revises requirements for milk provided by the National School Lunch Program of the Department of Agriculture (USDA) to allow schools to offer students whole and reduced-fat milk. The act also requires that local school food service personnel receive annual training and certification on food allergies.

The act permits schools to offer students whole, reduced-fat (2%), low-fat (1%), and fat-free flavored and unflavored milk. The milk that is offered may be organic or nonorganic. Currently, USDA regulations require milk to be fat-free or low-fat and allow milk to be flavored or unflavored. The act also removes the requirement that schools participating in the program must provide milk that is consistent with the most recent Dietary Guidelines for Americans.

The act also expands the nondairy beverages that are included in the program by allowing schools to offer all students nondairy beverages that are nutritionally equivalent to fluid milk and that meet nutritional standards established by USDA.

Further, schools currently must provide a substitute for fluid milk, on receipt of a written statement from a licensed physician, for students whose disability restricts their diet. Under the act, a parent or legal guardian may also provide the written statement.

In addition, the act excludes fluid milk from the saturated fat content calculation for school meals. Currently, schools participating in the program must provide meals that meet certain nutrition requirements; USDA regulations require that the average saturated fat content of the meals offered must be less than 10% of the total calories. Under the act, milk fat included in any fluid milk provided by the program must not be considered saturated fat for the purposes of measuring compliance with USDA regulations.

Finally, the program's mandatory training and certification for local school food service personnel must include a module on food allergies, including information on the best practices to prevent, recognize, and respond to food-related allergic reactions. Food service personnel must receive an annual certification to demonstrate competence in the food allergies training and other training modules that are provided.
